Clinical Reference

Acute Ischemic Stroke

On this page
Sudden focal neurologic deficit from arterial occlusion causing brain infarction (~87% of all strokes) — a time-critical emergency: the job is to restore perfusion to the salvageable penumbra before it dies.
BE-FAST → last-known-well tPA window ≤4.5 h · thrombectomy ≤24 h (selected) ~1.9 million neurons lost / minute Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg · TNK 0.25 mg/kg Door-to-needle ≤60 min
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

An artery to the brain occludes — usually a thrombus (on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque) or an embolus (most often from a fibrillating left atrium). Downstream tissue loses oxygen and glucose within seconds. Two zones form: an ischemic core where cerebral blood flow (CBF) is so low (<10–15 mL/100 g/min) that neurons are already dead, and a surrounding penumbra (CBF ~15–25) that is hypoperfused but still structurally intact — kept alive by collateral vessels. The penumbra is electrically silent but salvageable: it is the tissue every reperfusion therapy is racing to save. Without flow, the core steadily grows outward into the penumbra.

At the cellular level the excitotoxic cascade unfolds: ATP failure stalls the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → the membrane depolarizes → a flood of glutamate over-activates NMDA/AMPA receptors → calcium pours into neurons → proteases, lipases and free radicals dismantle the cell. Cytotoxic edema follows within hours; vasogenic edema and mass effect peak on days 2–5 and can herniate the brain (the "malignant" infarct).

A city after a water-main break. The core is the block where the pipe burst and the buildings already flooded and collapsed — unsalvageable. The penumbra is the surrounding neighborhood running on emergency reserve tanks (collaterals): the lights flicker but the buildings still stand — for now. Thrombolysis dissolves the clot in the main; thrombectomy is the crew physically hauling the debris out. Restore flow before the reserve tanks run dry and you save the district; arrive late and it's lost. Good cross-connected plumbing (good collaterals) is exactly why one patient still benefits at 24 hours and another doesn't at 4.
Time is brain — quantified. In a typical large-vessel supratentorial stroke the average patient loses ~1.9 million neurons, ~14 billion synapses, and ~12 km of myelinated fibers every minute; each untreated hour ages the brain ~3.6 years (Saver, Stroke 2006). That single number justifies every door-to-needle and door-to-groin metric.
The ischemic / excitotoxic cascade. The penumbra is the branch point — reperfuse in time and it lives; run out of collateral reserve and it joins the core.
Circle of Willis — the collateral ring. Cross-connections here (and leptomeningeal collaterals) determine how fast the core grows.
Brianwaichow, CC BY 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Gross specimen — established cerebral infarction (softened, discolored territory). This is the endpoint reperfusion aims to prevent.
علاء, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Every therapy in this guide maps to one step above. Alteplase / tenecteplase convert plasminogen → plasmin to lyse the fibrin clot (removes the occlusion). Thrombectomy physically extracts a large clot the lytic can't dissolve. Antiplatelets block platelet aggregation (COX-1/TXA₂; P2Y₁₂) to stop new atherothrombus. Statins stabilize plaque. Anticoagulation (DOAC/warfarin) prevents cardioembolic clot. BP / glucose / temperature control protect autoregulation and slow core growth into the penumbra.
📊

Presentation — signs by frequency & why they happen

Frequencies are approximate and vary by territory/cohort; anterior-circulation (MCA) strokes dominate (~80%). Color: red >70% · amber 40–70% · blue 15–40% · purple <15%.

Sign / symptom~FreqWhy it happens (mechanism)
Unilateral limb weakness / hemiparesis~80%Corticospinal tract / motor cortex (MCA, internal capsule) ischemia; contralateral to lesion
Facial droop (lower face)~45–60%Corticobulbar fibers to lower facial nucleus; forehead spared (upper face bilaterally innervated)
Speech disturbance (dysarthria / aphasia)~45–55%Dysarthria = bulbar/cerebellar; aphasia = dominant (usually left) MCA — Broca (frontal) or Wernicke (temporal)
Sensory loss / numbness~40–50%Somatosensory cortex / thalamocortical tracts; contralateral
Gaze deviation (toward lesion)~20–30%Frontal eye field ischemia — eyes "look at the lesion"; cortical sign suggesting LVO
Visual field cut (homonymous hemianopia)~20–30%Optic radiations (MCA/PCA) or occipital cortex (PCA)
Ataxia / incoordination / gait failure~20–30%Cerebellar or brainstem (posterior circulation) ischemia
Neglect / extinction (inattention)~15–25%Non-dominant (usually right) parietal MCA; cortical sign suggesting LVO
Vertigo, diplopia, dysphagia (crossed signs)~15–20%Vertebrobasilar / brainstem ischemia (e.g., lateral medullary / Wallenberg)
Depressed level of consciousness~10–15%Large hemispheric infarct with edema, bilateral/brainstem involvement, or basilar occlusion
Headache at onset~10–15%More with posterior-circulation / large infarcts; thunderclap suggests hemorrhage instead
Seizure at onset~3–5%Cortical irritation; a stroke mimic caveat (Todd paralysis post-ictal)
Cortical signs (gaze deviation, neglect, aphasia) plus a high NIHSS (≥6) predict a large-vessel occlusion — the patient who needs a thrombectomy center, not just tPA.

Pearls & pitfalls

💡

The 15 that change management

  1. Glucose is the first test and a classic mimic — always fingerstick before calling it a stroke; hypoglycemia (<50) and severe hyperglycemia produce focal deficits.
  2. The CT's acute job is to rule OUT hemorrhage, not rule IN infarct — an early ischemic CT can look normal; a normal CT does not delay thrombolysis.
  3. Time is brain — ~1.9 million neurons/min — every minute of door-to-needle / door-to-groin counts (Saver 2006).
  4. TNK is now co-equal to alteplase (2026) and easier — a single 0.25 mg/kg bolus, no 1-hour infusion → faster treatment and simpler drip-and-ship transfers.
  5. Give the lytic even if going to thrombectomy ("bridging") when eligible — don't skip IV thrombolysis for an EVT-eligible patient.
  6. Permissive hypertension — do NOT lower BP unless >220/120 (no reperfusion), or to reach the thresholds (185/110 pre-lytic, 180/105 post). Dropping BP starves the pressure-dependent penumbra; 2026 also warns against driving SBP <140 post-EVT.
  7. The late window is imaging-selected, not clock-selected — a good-collateral patient at 20 h can benefit while a bad-collateral patient at 4 h may not (DAWN/DEFUSE-3).
  8. Delay aspirin 24 h after thrombolysis (recheck NCCT first); otherwise start ASA within 24–48 h.
  9. Short-course DAPT only — ASA+clopidogrel for 21 days (or ASA+ticagrelor 30 days) then a single agent; long-term DAPT just bleeds.
  10. Screen swallowing before ANY PO — aspiration pneumonia is a leading preventable in-hospital complication.
  11. Malignant MCA edema peaks day 2–5 — anticipate it in large infarcts; hemicraniectomy <48 h in patients ≤60 saves lives; osmotherapy only temporizes.
  12. Cerebellar infarct is a surgical emergency in a small box — declining consciousness → suboccipital decompression + EVD.
  13. Reverse post-tPA ICH with cryoprecipitate 10 units (goal fibrinogen ≥150), TXA if cryo unavailable (2017 AHA statement).
  14. USPSTF says do NOT screen asymptomatic carotids (Grade D) — but symptomatic ≥70% stenosis gets CEA within 2 weeks.
  15. Cryptogenic/ESUS → hunt for AFib with prolonged monitoring (30-day patch or implantable loop) before defaulting to antiplatelet.
Stroke mimics (up to ~20% of "codes"): hypoglycemia, seizure with Todd paralysis, complicated migraine with aura, conversion/functional deficit, Bell palsy (forehead involved), toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, and unmasking of an old deficit by infection/fever. When the story or exam doesn't fit a vascular territory, reconsider — but do not let mimic-hunting delay reperfusion in a convincing stroke.
Chameleons are the opposite trap — real strokes that don't look like strokes: isolated vertigo (posterior circulation), acute confusion (dominant-hemisphere or thalamic), or a "spinal" pattern from a medial medullary infarct. Sudden onset plus a focal-anatomy story should keep stroke on the list.
🩺 Clinic — TIA, prevention & secondary risk reduction
Assess

TIA & when to route to the ED

🔍

Recognize the warning shot

A TIA is a transient focal deficit from ischemia without infarction (tissue-based definition; the old "<24 h" is time-based but most last minutes). It is a warning shot — the highest stroke risk is in the first 48 hours to 7 days. Evaluate the cause within 48 hours (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention).

BE-FAST — any sudden onset = call 911 Balance loss · Eyes (vision loss / diplopia) · Face drooping · Arm weakness · Speech difficulty · Time (note last-known-well, call immediately). The "BE" catches posterior-circulation strokes that plain FAST misses.
Do not "watch and wait" in clinic: any acute focal deficit, any TIA (even fully resolved), thunderclap headache, or decreased consciousness → 911 / ED now for urgent imaging + stroke evaluation.

Secondary prevention — the ladder

💊

Antithrombotic: match the mechanism

Non-cardioembolic (atherosclerotic / lacunar / cryptogenic) → antiplatelet (block platelet aggregation). Cardioembolic (AFib) → anticoagulation (block fibrin/thrombin generation). Antiplatelet does not substitute for anticoagulation in confirmed AFib.

2
Blood pressure, diabetes & lifestyle
Long-term BP <130/80; A1c individualized; smoking cessation
▾

BP target <130/80 (AHA/ASA 2021). Start/titrate a few days after the acute event, not hyperacutely. Agents: thiazide (chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg), ACEi/ARB (lisinopril 10→40 mg; losartan 50→100 mg), CCB (amlodipine 5→10 mg) — combine to goal.

Diabetes: A1c ~≤7% individualized; favor agents with CV/renal benefit (GLP-1 RA, SGLT2i). Smoking cessation (counseling + pharmacotherapy), Mediterranean diet, activity, weight, moderate/no alcohol, OSA screening — all Class 1.

3
Carotid revascularization (symptomatic stenosis)
CEA vs CAS thresholds
▾
  • Symptomatic ≥70% ICA stenosis → carotid endarterectomy (CEA), ideally within 2 weeks (NASCET: 17% absolute 2-yr stroke reduction).
  • Symptomatic 50–69% → CEA reasonable in selected patients (more benefit in men, older age, hemispheric events).
  • Symptomatic <50% → medical therapy only.
  • Carotid stenting (CAS) — alternative for high surgical risk / hostile neck; younger patients tolerate CAS better, older have more peri-procedural stroke.
Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Lipids 4–12 weeks after starting/changing statin, then annually — confirm LDL <70; add ezetimibe/PCSK9i if above.
  • BP at each visit to <130/80; home monitoring encouraged.
  • Adherence to antithrombotic/statin at every visit (non-adherence is a top cause of recurrence).
  • Rhythm — prolonged monitoring for cryptogenic/ESUS before defaulting to antiplatelet; if AFib found, convert to anticoagulation.
  • A1c per diabetes cadence; renal function for DOAC dosing.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change the plan

ComorbidityEffect on course & management
Atrial fibrillationDominant cardioembolic cause → anticoagulate (DOAC preferred; warfarin for mechanical valve / severe MS). Prior stroke already = CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2.
DiabetesHyperglycemia worsens infarct and hemorrhagic-transformation risk; higher recurrence → aggressive risk-factor control.
HypertensionLeading modifiable risk factor; chronic HTN shifts autoregulation rightward → don't crash BP acutely, target <130/80 long-term.
CKDDOAC dose-adjust/avoid at low CrCl; contrast-associated AKI with CTA (don't withhold emergent imaging for it).
Prior intracranial hemorrhageContraindicates thrombolysis; long-term antithrombotic is high-stakes (consider LAA closure for AFib if anticoagulation truly contraindicated).
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: long-term DAPT beyond 21–30 days (bleeds); routine antiplatelet + anticoagulant combination; sublingual/short-acting nifedipine (precipitous BP drops); overtreating BP in the first days after stroke (starves penumbra); starting anticoagulation before imaging-guided timing.

Escalate

Red flags → ED

🚑

Don't manage these in clinic

Any new focal deficit, recurrent TIA symptoms, a deficit that is worsening, thunderclap headache, or decreased consciousness → call 911. Note last-known-well time — it determines reperfusion eligibility. Do not give aspirin at home if a bleed hasn't been excluded by CT.
🛏️ Wards — hyperacute reperfusion & stroke-unit care
Admit

The hyperacute clock

📋

Every acute stroke is admitted — the question is how fast you reperfuse

On arrival: establish last-known-well (LKW), fingerstick glucose, calculate NIHSS, and get the patient to non-contrast CT immediately. Targets: door-to-CT ≤25 min, door-to-needle ≤60 min (ideally ≤45), door-to-groin as fast as possible for LVO. Admit all acute strokes to a stroke unit (organized stroke-unit care independently improves outcomes).

Hyperacute pathway. CT's first job is to exclude hemorrhage; a normal CT does not delay thrombolysis. Give the lytic and proceed to thrombectomy in eligible LVO ("bridging").

Why the labs move

LabWhy it matters / what shifts it
GlucoseHypo (<50) and severe hyperglycemia mimic stroke; hyperglycemia worsens infarct & hemorrhagic transformation. Confounders: steroids, DKA, sepsis.
Platelets / INR / aPTTGate thrombolysis (need plt ≥100k, INR ≤1.7, normal aPTT). Falsely reassuring INR does not exclude DOAC effect — ask about last DOAC dose (within 48 h contraindicates tPA).
TroponinMay rise from concurrent MI or demand ischemia/neurogenic stunning; doesn't delay reperfusion.
A1c / lipidsSet secondary-prevention targets; A1c reflects chronic glycemia (falsely low in hemolysis/blood loss, high in iron deficiency).

Hyperacute management ladder

💊

Reperfusion first, then the stroke-unit bundle

1
IV thrombolysis (≤4.5 h from LKW)
Alteplase or tenecteplase — memorize both doses
▾
AgentDoseAdministration → windowWhy it worksNotes
Alteplase (tPA)0.9 mg/kg, MAX 90 mg10% as bolus over 1 min, remaining 90% over 60 min; ≤4.5 hRecombinant plasminogen activator → plasmin → lyses fibrin clotClassic standard (NINDS ≤3 h; ECASS III 3–4.5 h)
Tenecteplase (TNK)0.25 mg/kg, MAX 25 mgsingle IV bolus ~5 s — no infusion; ≤4.5 hMore fibrin-specific, longer half-life → one bolus2026: co-equal Class 1 with alteplase, favored for single-bolus convenience & before thrombectomy (EXTEND-IA TNK)
Extended / wake-up: IV thrombolysis 4.5–9 h may be reasonable when perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue (EXTEND); wake-up strokes treat if DWI+ / FLAIR− (WAKE-UP). Correct glucose <50 before treating.
Absolute exclusions (abbreviated): any hemorrhage on CT or prior ICH; active internal bleeding; suspected SAH/endocarditis/dissection; ischemic stroke or serious head trauma in prior 3 months; recent intracranial/spinal surgery; BP >185/110 not lowerable; platelets <100k, INR >1.7, elevated aPTT, or DOAC within 48 h; glucose the cause of deficit; extensive early hypodensity.
1
Blood-pressure management (the tested numbers)
Depends entirely on whether you're reperfusing
▾
SituationTarget
Before IV thrombolysisLower to <185/110
During & 24 h after thrombolysisKeep <180/105
Not receiving reperfusion (permissive HTN)Do not lower unless >220/120; then cautious ~15% reduction over 24 h
Post-reperfusion (2026 caution)Avoid SBP <140 in first ~72 h post-thrombectomy (harm)
The penumbra has lost autoregulation and is pressure-dependent on collateral flow — dropping BP crashes penumbral perfusion and grows the infarct. When you must lower it, use titratable IV labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine. Avoid nitroprusside (raises ICP) and short-acting nifedipine.
2
Mechanical thrombectomy (LVO)
≤6 h standard; 6–24 h with imaging selection
▾
  • ≤6 h from LKW — anterior LVO (ICA/M1), ASPECTS ≥6, NIHSS ≥6, pre-stroke mRS 0–1 → Class 1 (MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND-IA, SWIFT PRIME, REVASCAT).
  • 6–24 h — selected anterior LVO meeting DAWN (clinical-core mismatch) or DEFUSE-3 (perfusion mismatch, 6–16 h).
  • 2026 expansions (Class 1): large-core ASPECTS 3–5 up to 24 h (age <80, NIHSS ≥6) and basilar occlusion NIHSS ≥10 up to 24 h.
  • Bridging: give IV thrombolysis in eligible patients even if going to thrombectomy — don't skip the lytic.
2

Monitor

What to trend daily

📈

Daily stroke-unit checklist

  • Neuro exam / NIHSS — a ≥4-point rise or new pupil asymmetry → STAT NCCT (hemorrhage? malignant edema?).
  • BP to the situation-specific target; glucose 140–180; temperature (treat fever).
  • Swallow status before advancing diet; aspiration precautions.
  • Mobility / early rehab (PT/OT/SLP); skin, bowel/bladder, VTE prophylaxis.
  • Etiology workup progress — telemetry, echo, carotids; plan secondary prevention.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers (numeric)

Transfer to ICU for: post-thrombolysis monitoring (first ~24 h); post-thrombectomy; NIHSS rise ≥4 or declining consciousness (GCS drop); large hemispheric or cerebellar infarct with edema / malignant-MCA features; airway compromise (GCS ≤8, failure to protect); seizures/status; hemodynamic instability requiring drips; symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation; BP uncontrollable on the ward.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: neurologically/medically stable; secondary-prevention meds started (antithrombotic, high-intensity statin, BP plan, anticoagulation if AFib); swallow cleared or plan (e.g., PEG); rehab needs assessed by PT/OT/SLP; follow-up and risk-factor plan in place.

Home

Independent, mRS ≤1–2, minimal deficit.

Home health

Home + skilled nursing / outpatient therapy visits.

SNF

Needs 24 h nursing, lower-intensity rehab (<3 h/day tolerable).

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines — best functional-recovery setting for moderate deficits.

LTAC

Prolonged complex medical needs (e.g., vent weaning, tracheostomy).

Hospice / palliative

Devastating stroke; comfort-focused, goals-of-care.
🫀 ICU — neurocritical care & edema management
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When stroke belongs in the unit

Post-thrombolysis intensive monitoring; post-thrombectomy; large hemispheric ("malignant") MCA infarct; cerebellar infarct with mass effect / 4th-ventricle compression; depressed consciousness / airway risk (GCS ≤8); hemodynamic instability requiring pressors; symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation; status epilepticus; need for ICP management or osmotherapy.

Monitor

Monitoring, access & BP

🩸

Neuro checks are the monitor

Post-alteplase BP + neuro checks: q15 min ×2 h → q30 min ×6 h → q1 h ×16 h (24 h total). Frequent NIHSS / GCS / pupils; a ≥4-point NIHSS rise or new pupil asymmetry → STAT NCCT.

BP situationTarget
Post-reperfusion (first 24 h)Keep <180/105; 2026: avoid SBP <140 ×72 h post-EVT (harm)
Not reperfused (permissive HTN)Treat only if >220/120
Hypotension / hypovolemiaHarmful (↓collateral flow) — give isotonic fluids, treat cause; pressor if needed

Titratable IV agents: nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol. Arterial line for labile BP / drips; central access for hypertonic saline or pressors. Head-of-bed 30°, normocapnia, isotonic (0.9% NaCl) fluids only — no hypotonic fluids or dextrose (worsen edema/hyperglycemia).

Rescue

Malignant edema, surgery & reversal

⚙️

The neurosurgical & osmotic playbook

1
Decompressive hemicraniectomy (malignant MCA)
Life-saving when early & young
▾

Malignant MCA infarct = large (often >50% MCA territory) infarct with progressive edema → midline shift, herniation; peaks day 2–5; ~70–80% mortality with medical therapy alone.

Hemicraniectomy <48 h of onset in patients ≤60 y markedly reduces mortality and improves functional survival — pooled DESTINY/DECIMAL/HAMLET: survival with mRS ≤4 rose 75% vs 24%. Benefit in >60 y (DESTINY II) is real for survival but with more moderate–severe disability → goals-of-care discussion. Counsel families: it trades death for survival, often with disability.

Large MCA-territory infarction — the substrate for malignant edema and hemicraniectomy.
Lucien Monfils, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia
2
Osmotic therapy (temporizing — bridge to surgery)
Mannitol / hypertonic saline
▾
AgentDoseTitration / targetWhy it worksWatch
Mannitol0.25–1 g/kg IV bolusRepeat q4–6 h; follow serum osm / osmolal gapOsmotic gradient pulls water out of brainHypovolemia, AKI, rebound; check osm gap
Hypertonic saline 23.4%30 mL IV over 10–15 min (central line)For acute herniation; recheck examSteep osmotic gradient; also volume-expands (better for hypotension than mannitol)Central access required; monitor Na
Hypertonic saline 3% infusionTitrateTarget Na 145–155Sustained osmotic therapy for edema controlAvoid rapid overcorrection
Osmotherapy only temporizes — it is a bridge to definitive decompression, not a substitute. Adjuncts: head-of-bed 30°, normocapnia, treat fever/seizure, avoid hypotonic fluids.
2
Cerebellar infarct with mass effect
A surgical emergency in a small box
▾

The posterior fossa is a tight compartment — swelling → brainstem compression + obstructive hydrocephalus (4th ventricle) → rapid deterioration. Watch for declining consciousness → suboccipital decompressive craniectomy (± infarct removal) and EVD for hydrocephalus; often good outcome because the brainstem itself is spared.

3
Hemorrhagic transformation after tPA — reversal
Stop lytic, correct fibrinogen
▾

Suspect if sudden neuro decline, new headache, HTN, N/V, ↑NIHSS during/after lytic → STOP the lytic, STAT NCCT, STAT labs (CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, type & cross). Per AHA/ASA 2017 statement:

  • Cryoprecipitate 10 units IV (first line if thrombolytic in prior 24 h) → recheck fibrinogen; goal fibrinogen ≥150 mg/dL, give more if below.
  • If cryo unavailable → antifibrinolytic: tranexamic acid 10–15 mg/kg IV over ~20 min or ε-aminocaproic acid 4–5 g IV.
  • Reverse any other anticoagulant, control BP, neurosurgery consult.
Support

Pressors (if maintaining perfusion)

💉

Not routine — for hypotension or induced-HTN trials

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
NorepinephrinePotent α₁ + modest β₁0.01–0.5+ mcg/kg/min↑SVR/MAP, mild ↑COFirst-line to raise/maintain MAP & collateral support
PhenylephrinePure α₁ (reflex bradycardia, no inotropy)40–180 mcg/min (or 50–200 mcg boluses)↑SVR/MAPWhen tachyarrhythmia limits norepi; quick BP raise for induced-HTN trial
DopamineDose-dependent DA/β/α5–20 mcg/kg/min↑CO & SVRMore arrhythmia — generally not first choice
Cerebral perfusion pressure to the penumbra is pressure-dependent — hypotension is harmful. Norepinephrine's α₁ vasoconstriction raises MAP with modest β₁ support; phenylephrine's pure α₁ avoids tachycardia. Induced hypertension is not routine; if trialed for fluctuating pressure-dependent deficits, do it in ICU with close neuro monitoring.
Airway

Airway, ventilation & ICP

🌬️

Protect the airway, protect the brain

Intubate for depressed consciousness (GCS ≤8), failure to protect the airway, or malignant edema. Avoid hypoxia and hyper/hypocapnia — target normocapnia; brief hyperventilation only as a herniation-rescue bridge to definitive therapy. Elevate head of bed 30°, treat fever/pain/agitation. Seizure prophylaxis only if seizures occur (no routine prophylactic anticonvulsants).

Mode
AC/VC
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6–8 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective
PaCO₂
35–40
normocapnia (avoid low → vasoconstriction)
SpO₂ / PaO₂
>94% / ≥60
avoid hypoxia; no routine hyperoxia
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the stroke unit

Downgrade when: 24 h post-lytic monitoring completed with no hemorrhage on follow-up imaging and a stable exam; no rising NIHSS; off pressors; airway secure/extubated; edema peak passed without herniation (usually past day 5); BP controlled on non-titratable oral meds; swallow assessed.

Not yet if: still within the malignant-edema window with a large infarct, requiring hypertonic-saline boluses, labile on IV drips, or any new neuro decline.
